entries.title: Muse, Meta's New Personal AI Agent, Needs You to Trust It
entries.summary: Designed to compete with OpenClaw and Instinct, the company says Muse can do everything from sell your car to book you a plane ticket.
entries.content:
Meta announced Tuesday the release of Muse, a personal AI agent that people can message to automate digital tasks in a secure cloud environment, all while relying on security and privacy that the company says is “built into it” from the start.

Meta says Muse is rolling out today for iOS and Android users in a dedicated Muse app, as well as the website Muse.ai. The company also says users can directly message Muse in WhatsApp to interact with the agent. Meta says users of its AI glasses will soon be able to interact with its Muse agent as well. Meta says people can try out Muse for free, but users who want to automate lots of digital tasks will need one of the company’s AI subscription plans.

Muse is Meta’s latest attempt to compete with viral AI agents such as OpenClaw and Instinct, which users can message with to automate digital tasks. Muse is a product of Meta Superintelligence Labs, the AI unit CEO Mark Zuckerberg formed roughly a year ago to catch up with OpenAI and Anthropic, offering some researchers eye-popping compensation packages to join. The unit was built on the belief that AI agents will transform how everyday users navigate the internet, as well as Meta’s products.

WIRED previously reported that Meta has been testing Muse internally under the codename “Hatch,” and that employees have been using it to autonomously operate third-party applications and browse the web on their behalf.

Meta claims in a blog post that anyone can use Muse out of the box, and that the product was designed “so there’s no learning curve.” The company says users can prompt Muse in natural language, and the agent will work on its own to send emails, book travel, or even help sell a car on a user’s behalf.

Muse is also capable of making purchases on behalf of users, checking out using special payment infrastructure designed by Stripe. The payment tool, which Stripe calls Link, issues a single-use card number so that agents aren’t going around entering a person’s real financial information across the internet. Meta says Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections for agents, which guarantees no-fee returns.

Meta is late to release a personal agent, but it seems to be seeking to differentiate itself by focusing on security and privacy features for Muse. The agent is debuting with an architecture for all users dubbed Secure VM, which is meant to isolate each user’s activity in a so-called virtual machine to keep untrusted data from the web and any integrations separate from the part of the agent that can actually take action on a user’s behalf.

A personal AI agent requires a lot of user trust, something Meta in particular has struggled with significantly over the years. To get users to try out Muse—and allow the agent to be integrated with users’ third-party apps and services—Meta is attempting to convince people that they can trust the company to handle their data appropriately.

“We know it’s really important, if we’re going to build a product like this that can access a lot of sources of personal data, that we’re really responsible with that, so we’ve designed this system very deliberately,” says David Singleton, Meta Superintelligence Lab’s vice president of engineering for consumer products. “And we’ve built what we call the Sentinel that actually looks out for everything that’s moving out of the VM and either matches it to an existing policy where the user or the system has given permission for that to happen or presents a human-in-the-loop dialog to ask you to approve the action it’s going to take.”

Singleton notes that these check-in prompts for humans come directly to the user and aren’t filtered through the model, to protect against attacks like prompt injections.

While Secure VM is built to maintain user security and privacy, it is not a truly locked box. Singleton notes that while Meta is barred by policy from accessing user Muse data, it would still be technically possible. Users can opt out of allowing their data to be used for training.

The architecture of Secure VM is noteworthy from a privacy standpoint, if only as a way to set a new industry standard for AI agents. Eventually, Meta will also offer Muse “Confidential VM,” designed so each VM runs in a “trusted execution environment” and users manage their own access keys locally on their devices. This way no one else, including Meta, can access that user’s agent VM.

Confidential VM comes as part of Meta’s work with Moxie Marlinspike, creator of the end-to-end encrypted messaging app Signal who also developed the privacy-focused AI platform Confer in recent years.

WIRED viewed an advance draft of a technical white paper describing Confidential VM. In addition to structuring the system so the user controls their access keys, Meta is also giving select security firms access to the Confidential VM source to regularly audit and verify its privacy guarantees. Meta will also publish the Confidential VM binaries (machine-readable instruction files) and a transparency log, so users can verify the validity and integrity of their connection to Muse.

Singleton emphasizes that Muse Secure VM has already been extensively vetted, including by Meta’s human and agentic red teams as well as through the company’s private bug bounty. And now Meta is adding Muse to the scope of its public bounty as well, with payouts up to $300,000 for valid vulnerability findings, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt injection attacks that affect a single user.

entries.title: Apple and Google Miss Deadline to Block Child Nudity on Their Phones in the UK
entries.summary: Now the UK government plans to introduce new legislation that would see companies face fines and potential criminal liability, and signaled similar plans could extend to Snapchat and Instagram.
entries.content:
In June, the UK government told Big Tech it had three months to make taking, viewing, or sharing images of child nudity on their devices impossible. “I expect tech firms to make that happen,” said then prime minister Keir Starmer. “But if they choose not to, then we will act and change the law.”

That deadline arrived on Tuesday, and the government says that the likes of Apple and Google have failed. As a result, they will be changing the law to introduce what the UK government claims will be world-first legislation of its kind.

While engineers from Apple and Google had been working with the government since June to make changes, “they do not meet the scale of this crisis,” Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media, and sport, told lawmakers on Tuesday as she introduced the legislation.

Under the new plan, companies failing to build the child protection solutions into all existing and newly sold smartphones and tablets in the UK would face fines and potential criminal liability for their bosses. “We know that this is a sector that can—when required—innovate at an extraordinary pace when the chips are down,” Nandy added.

Nandy also plans to explore placing similar legal requirements on apps used by children, like Instagram and Snapchat. Neither Meta nor Snap immediately responded to a request for comment.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from the worst harms,” Nandy said, “and to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace we need it to while harm is being done now.” Still, she said she would reassess whether legislation is necessary if platforms implement solutions while it is being drawn up.

“Apple and Google needed to urgently introduce these protections to ensure online sexual abuse is disrupted and prevented on children’s devices,” says Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. “Now the deadline is up, government must crack down and legislate.”

Not everyone is so keen on the measures, which would not impact adults who had verified their age. In June, messaging app Signal accused the UK government of using the measures to rush “invisible surveillance infrastructure” into law. It warned that forcing UK residents to prove their age and have their content scanned in the name of child safety could be a slippery slope into wider surveillance.

Apple, meanwhile, says it is working with the UK government in the name of protecting kids. “We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe,” an Apple spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement, pointing to its Communication Safety feature launched in 2021, which blurs photos or videos detected to contain nudity on a child's device.

A Google spokesperson says in a statement that their team is “pleased to have made progress and are fully committed to continuing to work with experts, legislators, app developers and device manufacturers to keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information.”

Globally, governments taking more extreme measures to protect children from online harms have been met with backlash over privacy and other digital rights. In the European Union, civil rights activists opposed extended legislation allowing tech firms to voluntarily scan users’ private messages for child sexual abuse material. Elon Musk’s X complained that the information-gathering powers imposed by Australia’s social media ban risk interfering with international law.

In the UK, Nandy also said the government was considering going further with its sweeping social media ban for children under 16, which was announced earlier this year and remains on track to go into effect in spring 2027. She is also looking at strengthening the law around AI chatbots to protect children on those platforms as well.

entries.title: OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul
entries.summary: A landmark announcement by the frontier AI lab has been overshadowed by accusations of impropriety.
entries.content:
OpenAI said today that it has found an AI-generated solution to one of the biggest problems in mathematics—a 200-year-old equation that describes the natural behavior of fluids like water and air.

The announcement appears to demonstrate the stunning power for AI to advance mathematics. But it has been marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of the work of Buckmaster and a colleague—Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. Buckmaster claims OpenAI also tried to influence who got credit for the work.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former OpenAI employee or mathematician who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at mzeff.88 and wak.01.

The proof concerns the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the unsolved problems in the Clay Millennium prizes, which are each worth $1 million.

Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the company began training a new AI model with advanced mathematical capabilities on August 28.

After reading rumors that Anthropic was making progress toward solving Navier-Stokes, Bubeck said the company decided to dedicate more resources to tackling the problem. The company had more than 1,000 agents tackle the problem over more than 50 hours before discovering that it had come up with a solution.

“I thought there must be a mistake somewhere,” Bubeck said. “And on Sunday morning we had the final solution, Lean-formalized and everything.” (Lean is a programming language that can be used to formalize mathematical proofs.)

OpenAI noted that solving this problem required using considerably more computing power than it had previously spent on solving mathematical problems. The amount required cost “in the millions of dollars,” said Mark Chen, head of research at OpenAI.

On Monday, Alpöge and Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, posted documents claiming key advances in an area relevant to the Navier-Stokes problem. The pair says they used several AI models, including Claude and Codex, to complete their work.

Buckmaster also posted a statement claiming that, last week, he learned that OpenAI had become aware of his and Alpöge’s work and had started putting significant resources toward the problem. Buckmaster claims that he asked OpenAI leaders about whether the company had accessed the pair’s Codex logs. He says he was told the model “didn’t look up user data” but claims the company didn’t respond to questions about training. He then says that OpenAI offered several “proposals,” including one in which Buckmaster could publish a paper announcing the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by an internal OpenAI model but without Alpöge’s name included.

In a post on social media, Bubeck pushed back on the idea that the company had suggested removing Alpöge’s name. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also stepped into the fight, and defended the team's work.

Buckmaster, Alpöge, and Anthropic did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

In the briefing, Bubeck and other OpenAI executives denied that the company had ever inspected the pair’s Codex prompts in order to inform their work. “We, whether it’s the researchers or the agents, did not see any of their work until it was released publicly last night,” he said.

In a blog post detailing the work, the company wrote, “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠.”

“I want to be extremely clear that we recognize the priority of Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s work on unforced Euler, and we have nothing but congratulations to them on this monumental achievement that they have made. To be clear, we did not use their prompt or proof to prompt our models or direct our agents,” said Bubeck.

Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company, also emphasized that their solution was significantly different in nature from the one produced by OpenAI’s model.

The spat over who gets credit for solving one of the biggest problems in math may rumble on for a while. As AI takes on more of the work involved with finding proofs, such fights could perhaps become more common.

entries.title: Here’s Samsung’s Advice for Apple and Its Upcoming Folding iPhone
entries.summary: The competition is “absolutely welcome” by the pioneering Korean giant, but Samsung warns that the device’s “weight” is crucial.
entries.content:
On the eve of Apple’s highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung isn’t feeling threatened. Instead, the folding smartphone pioneer says the competition is “absolutely welcome.”

That’s according to Hee-Cheul Moon, head of Samsung’s Advanced Mechanical R&D Group, who sat with WIRED on a virtual Zoom call with Seungki Choi, head of Samsung’s Smartphone R&D Group. Before the talk veered toward Apple, the pair spoke about how the company managed to shave 75 grams off the weight of its latest Galaxy Z Fold8 in the seven years since it debuted the original.

Weight is integral to a folding phone’s success. If the device is too chunky and heavy, you’re less likely to want to use it. Over the past two years, folding devices from Honor, Google, and Samsung have rapidly gotten lighter, with each iteration featuring thinner designs. It may be why Samsung saw preorders for its latest folding handsets increase 30 percent globally versus last year’s models, with the Fold8—the device with a new smaller shape that’s easier to hold—accounting for nearly half.

“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says through a translator.

When I asked what advice the company had for Apple ahead of its folding debut, Moon said, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it’s not easy." Apple’s folding iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Ultra, is expected to weigh between 230 and 241 grams (the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233 grams), heftier than Samsung’s latest.

Samsung has made notable strides this year in making its main Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone lighter than top-end candybar-shaped smartphones. The single-screen Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214 grams, but the Fold8 is merely 201 grams, thanks to its smaller, passport-style shape. The company says its own customer data and YouGov survey data from 2024 show that bulky designs were a chief concern for people uninterested in folding phones.

The company says it analyzed every single component in the latest Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra—approximately 270 components and more than 180 auxiliary parts—from circuit boards and antennas to tapes and fastening components.

The team looked everywhere to cut weight. For example, it redesigned the printed circuit board to remove unnecessary circuits and improve component layout, reducing the space requirement. Samsung says it even eliminated 15 auxiliary parts and machined the internal display support plate down to roughly 0.2 millimeters. To keep that thinner panel durable, Samsung developed its “Flex Titanium” screen—a titanium alloy film roughly one-third the width of a human hair designed to maintain surface flatness and keep the crease from worsening over years of folding.

You’ll also notice Samsung’s primary folding phone no longer has three cameras on the back. Instead, it’s powered by a dual-camera system, a main camera and an ultrawide—there’s no more telephoto. For those who still demand high-end zoom and a 200-megapixel primary shooter, Samsung points to the larger Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, framing the Fold8’s camera cutback as an intentional concession to deliver that lightweight, passport-style design.

Apple’s folding iPhone is also expected to have a wider and shorter passport-style shape, and it’s likely to have a similar camera setup. Both Apple and Samsung made similar concessions last year chasing ultrathin and light smartphones.

Choi says this came down to user feedback as Samsung’s customers wanted a folding device that was “effortlessly portable” yet could be unfolded for an immersive multimedia experience. “We continue to always monitor the voice from the market, and we are open to any possibilities,” he says. We spend most of our time consuming multimedia with our smartphones, and the Fold8’s new shape is specifically tailored for media, with less obvious letterboxing than previous Folds.

Yet chasing that slim, lightweight profile leaves foldables exposed where traditional flagships excel: durability and ingress protection. Most candybar smartphones sport an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, meaning they’ll be fine even after spending some time at the bottom of a pool, but the Galaxy Z Fold8 series is still stuck at IP48—it can get wet, but dust will cause problems. Dust notoriously forced Samsung to delay the launch of the first Galaxy Fold in 2019, as little specks could get through the hinge and damage the screen.

Google’s folding Pixels are the only models with an IP68 rating. Still, even with the higher rating, dust can pose a problem, according to Elizabeth Chamberlain, iFixit’s director of Sustainability. The repair company’s teardowns show that dust can get inside the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, making the hinge sound “crunchy” and causing what could be a serious liability over time.

“We still haven’t seen a solution for that,” Chamberlain tells WIRED. “Repair is still a problem for foldables.” iFixit’s recent teardown of the Galaxy Z Fold8 gave it a 4/10 for repairability. “The hinge is buried under all the other components, and the hinge is the thing most likely to get damaged,” Chamberlain says. She did give Samsung props for its new adhesive system that makes battery removal easier.

Moon reiterated that Samsung’s Folds have the “best-in-class” dustproof and waterproof performance in the industry and that the company isn’t just “chasing the numbers for the sake of it.” He also emphasized that, despite the Fold8’s slim profile, internal components are far easier to detach and service than in earlier iterations.

That tension between engineering finesse and long-term durability is what Apple is stepping into. While Samsung enjoys a boost in Fold8 preorders, the broader foldable category was staring down a double-digit decline after five consecutive quarters of losing steam.

Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, says this niche market is stabilizing, and the upcoming iPhone is expected to help the category grow nearly 13 percent year over year—the only bit of growth in the smartphone market right now. Drew Blackard, Samsung’s senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, previously told WIRED that more competition will help bring visibility to the category.

Popal says foldables are more durable and dependable now, arguing Apple is entering just as hardware anxieties have eased.

Chamberlain isn’t convinced the category is truly mature. “I want a phone that is durable and repairable, and I think it’s highly unlikely that Apple will have solved the hinge problem,” she says.

Even with the durability question unanswered, Samsung’s engineers believe they’ve finally landed on the right formula. When I asked what device everyone in the room was using, a sea of Galaxy Z Fold8 models appeared in the air. Moon held up both the Z Fold8 and the Fold8 Ultra, smiling and saying, “We use the Fold8 Ultra also.”

entries.title: Richard Kelly on Donnie Darko at 25: ‘It’s a Miracle That Any Movie Gets Made’
entries.summary: The director discusses his debut novel, staying true to an artistic vision, and the absurd line of dialogue from Donnie Darko he believes will find its way into his obituary.
entries.content:
For a diehard fan of Donnie Darko, meeting director and screenwriter Richard Kelly is a thrill in itself. But to first encounter him as a silhouette in a darkened movie theater is to feel almost like a character in one of his films—unmoored by indefinite space and physics, questioning your altered perception.

It’s a hot Friday in mid-August when I sit down with Kelly, 51, at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre, a beloved repertory venue that makes a key appearance in Donnie Darko, his remarkable debut feature. Released in October 2001 with virtually no marketing due to the tragic events of 9/11 weeks prior (the plot hinges on a plane accident), it couldn’t get a toehold at the box office. But in the months and years that followed, the film became a hit on the home video market and gained a fervent cult fandom thanks to its unique supernatural mystery.

To mark its 25th anniversary, Fathom Entertainment will mount a limited theatrical rerelease of the film in a new 4K presentation, complete with a special introduction by Kelly—he’s just wrapped recording when I walk into the Aero. Screenings begin on October 2, the date that launches mentally disturbed suburban teenager Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal) on a surreal journey that may or may not lead to the end of the world. Snippets of the movie play without sound as Kelly and I settle into a back row to talk.

“My memories of this film run the entire spectrum from fear to love,” Kelly jokes, alluding to the corny pop psychology peddled by Patrick Swayze’s self-help guru in the film. This occasion, Kelly says, is all about the “love,” as he couldn’t be more grateful to “all the people who have continued to support” his work.

That camp should be pleased to hear that on December 15, Kelly will publish his mammoth first novel, The Philosophy of Time Travel, available for preorder now. The 800-page volume picks up right where the movie left off and is intended to set the stage for a film sequel as well. “It’s been very inspiring for me to remain focused on continuing the journey that began 25 years ago, on my own creative terms,” Kelly says. “This film has defined my entire career, but at the same time, it’s set a benchmark in the sense of the movies that I want to continue to make.”

Here, the auteur revisits the unforgettable dreamscape that put him on the map, and considers the artistic possibilities still ahead.

On when he realized Donnie Darko was becoming a cult hit:

There was one specific moment, I think in March of 2002, when I was in New York City. I was walking through the East Village, and I walked past a pizza restaurant called Two Boots, and my poster for Donnie Darko was hanging in their window. I saw the poster and I was like, “What’s going on? This is bizarre. Why does a pizza restaurant have a movie poster?” I went inside and I asked the manager, and he said, “Well, we have a little theater in the back, the Pioneer, and we’re playing your movie every Saturday night at midnight—and it’s selling out.”

I showed up the next Saturday night at about two in the morning, when the movie was finishing. I expected there’d be maybe 10 people there, and he wasn't joking, it was sold out, and there were people with camcorders and lights in my face, and Michael Musto from the Village Voice was there. I was just completely bowled over by the fact that there were people who cared, who were really, really connecting with the movie. That was the moment I knew that it wasn’t over, that the movie was going to have a second wind.

On how Drew Barrymore and Jason Schwartzman saved the screenplay from Hollywood purgatory:

It all started with Jason Schwartzman. He attached to play Donnie, and by virtue of his attachment, the script got sent around to a whole new round of people. It had been circulating for about a year, and the story was, “Oh, the writer won’t sell it. He wants to direct. It's his first movie, it’s too ambitious. It’s just a writing sample, he’s never gonna get that movie made. He won’t let anyone else take it away from him.”

Then the script got sent to Nancy Juvonen, who’s partners with Drew Barrymore [at Flower Films]. She read it and flipped out and wanted to meet me, so we went down to the set of Charlie’s Angels. We went into Drew Barrymore’s trailer, and she was finishing the script, and we just immediately hit it off. I’m like, “Drew, would you like to play the English teacher, Mrs. Pomeroy?” And she’s like, “Will you let my company, Flower Films, produce the movie with you? And I’m like, “Of course.” She had a one week window in August of 2000 before she was going to do a Penny Marshall film called Riding in Cars with Boys. We had to meet that deadline and get Drew to shoot her out in one week.

Jason Schwartzman had a scheduling conflict, and then in walks Jake Gyllenhaal. So it all happened really quickly. Nancy and Drew really deserve an enormous share of the credit in getting this whole thing off the ground—and Jason Schwartzman, too. Had he not attached, I would not have a career.

On having real-life siblings Jake and Maggie Gyllenhaal anchor a fictional on-screen family.

I heard from Joseph Middleton and Michelle Morris Gertz, our wonderful casting directors—they told me that Jake has an older sister, her name is Maggie Gyllenhaal, and she’s a brilliant actress. She had only appeared in one movie thus far, Cecil B. Demented, a John Waters film. I think she had a tiny cameo, but she had done a lot of theater and was obviously an enormous talent, like her brother, and once I realized there was a possibility of getting her, I was just like, “We have to get Maggie. It will anchor the family with real siblings, and Maggie will be this great foundation for Jake, and for the whole cast, and she was just so essential.” Sometimes the cards are dealt in your favor in terms of who’s available, who is interested, and so much of filmmaking is just the timing. It’s a miracle that any movie gets made.

On giving Seth Rogen his first film role (as a high school bully):

He had done Freaks and Geeks, and he was a standup comedian, performing in comedy clubs. Seth was one of these prodigy kids, really wise beyond his years and ahead of the game. He was maybe 19 years old when we shot the movie, the same age as Jake—incredibly observant, very articulate and funny young actor and writer and comedian, he was already pursuing all these different avenues. I felt like we had access to all the cool LA kid actors, because we shot in Los Angeles, it was the summer of 2000, and there was a commercial [actors] strike where all of the commercials were dark.

On creating the 1980s setting of Donnie Darko.

When we were doing the ‘80s, it was the year 2000, and we were capturing 1988, which is completely insane. That’s 12 years. So you subtract 12 years from 2026 and we are in 2014, which seems completely insane to do a period piece about 2014, because things don’t look that different than they did in 2014—but the disparity between 2000 and 1988 aesthetically was pretty significant. The cars looked completely different, the TVs looked different, the clothing looked different.

In terms of the ’80s aesthetic, we wanted it to feel subtle, we didn’t want a lot of big ’80s hair, and we didn’t want someone wearing a “Beat It” Michael Jackson jacket. We didn’t want it to be kitschy. April Ferry, our incredible, Oscar-nominated costume designer, who we lost a few years ago, was so wonderful in bringing the ’80s fashion for Mary McDonnell and Beth Grant—you see them with the shoulder pads and the different ’80s suburban costuming.

On the movie reference from his original script that didn’t make it to the screen:

In the original script, Donnie and Gretchen went to go see C.H.U.D., just because I thought it was a funny ’80s horror movie. Linda McDonough, who was an executive at Flower Films, was trying to track down the licensing permission for the movie C.H.U.D. as we were approaching the shoot date here at the Aero Theatre, and she was getting nowhere. It was one of the big studios, and there was some woman in charge of licensing at that studio who was just like, “You’re never getting this.”

You would think we were trying to license Lawrence of Arabia or Citizen Kane. They wanted so much money, and we were three days from shooting the scene, and we didn’t have a movie to show. Linda, to her enormous credit, said, “Richard, I am friends with the producers at the studio that owns The Evil Dead, they own the negative. Sam Raimi is a great guy, and they will let us have the poster to show at the front in the lobby of the theater. They’ll let you show any clip from The Evil Dead you want, the music, you can have it basically for free.” It was like a deus ex machina in the form of Sam Raimi. That led to the whole Evil Dead sequence in the movie, that was so perfect. Then we were able to do the marquee with The Last Temptation of Christ—we weren’t showing a clip from the Scorsese film or the poster, just showing the title. That’s an easier ask.

On the influential soundtrack of post-punk and new wave music:

I wasn’t thinking that deep. I was just like, “I love this song.” Like, “Head Over Heels” [by Tears for Fears] was written into the script because I knew that when Donnie and his friends jump out of the school bus, when Donnie’s feet hit the pavement, that first big piano note of “Head Over Heels” starts. When the camera flies through the window and you see all the kids sitting down and Drew Barrymore gathering the class together … “Time flies.” I had to get from the feet hitting the pavement to when they said, “Time flies,” and I had to edit the song down. It was just me doing a music video and loving that song and the vibe and the energy of it.

I have to give an enormous amount of credit to Manish Raval and Tom Wolfe, my music supervisors, who really expanded the canvas of the music in the movie to include Joy Division and Echo and the Bunnymen. It really did form a cohesive musical narrative. We were very fortunate, because no one was really trying to license a lot of that music in the year 2000.

The one song that we could not get—if you go back and watch the dailies, the Sparkle Motion dance scene was choreographed to Pet Shop Boys, but that was a no-go, we could not afford it, so we replaced it with Duran Duran.

On the dialogue that has had a surprising impact—such as the line “Sometimes I doubt your commitment to Sparkle Motion,” as delivered by actor Beth Grant:

It’s so ridiculous. You never know it’s gonna connect. Literally that’s gonna be in my obituary, that line of dialogue, the only thing people remember that I wrote. Beth Grant is the best.

On what the social media reaction would be like if Donnie Darko came out today:

I can’t even wrap my head around it. Online discourse is terrifying, and you kind of try to stay away from it. Any filmmaker that gets too caught up in online discourse, that can only have a negative impact on one’s art. You have to be cognizant of what’s going on in the world, but I think you need to curate your own art as the artist. We need more of that, art that is purely what the artist wants to say.

But I’m emboldened and excited about the younger generation going back to the theaters and reading books. Launching a book, the enormous amount of work that’s gone into writing a novel—it’s very gratifying to get to the finish line on something like that because you realize how a novel can help be the engine for something that is very difficult to get made because of the budget.

On the newer films and filmmakers to catch his eye:

Like everyone else, I saw Obsession. I thought it was terrific. Incredibly well done for such a small budget. The performances were great. I love Ari Aster’s work. I love Jane Schoenbrun’s work. I’ve not seen [Sex and Death at] Camp Miasma, that’s next on my list.

On the movie he most wants to make (besides a sequel to Donnie Darko):

There are so many scripts I’ve written and projects that have hit roadblocks for various reasons. I would love to get my Rod Serling biopic made. That is a very ambitious project that tells the life story of Rod Serling using a fantasy and science-fiction language, in conjunction with his daughter Anne Serling and her memoir about her father. It’s an expensive movie to make, given the fantasy elements and the period elements and the scope. If there are big influences, they would be Defending Your Life, the Albert Brooks film, A Matter of Life and Death by Powell and Pressberger, and All That Jazz by Bob Fosse.

Update on Tuesday, September 8 at 1:30 pm: This story was updated with more information about the 25th anniversary release and to add a link to buy tickets.

entries.title: Meta Failed to Catch Hundreds of AI Child Abuse Ads. Some Included Images of Real Kids
entries.summary: Images of real children—including a member of a European royal family—were used to create some of the 350 ads containing child sexual abuse. Lawmakers say they plan to investigate.

Editor’s note: This article contains descriptions of imagery depicting child sexual abuse. Reader discretion is strongly advised.

Early last month, Meta deleted around 50 ads posted on Facebook, Instagram, and Threads that directly included child sexual abuse material (CSAM), following reporting by WIRED. At the time, the company said that most of the abusive ads had been published prior to it rolling out new AI tools designed to “better detect and block” harmful ads being uploaded. That AI system, however, doesn’t appear to have been entirely effective.

Instead of spotting a decline in the abusive ads in recent weeks, researchers say they have now discovered hundreds more of the disturbing ads containing graphic sexual scenes involving children—including some that were identical to those Meta recently removed. More than 250 additional ads containing CSAM have run across Meta’s social media platforms since the start of August, according to researchers at the nonprofit Tech Transparency Project who shared its findings with WIRED. Unlike the 53 ads TTP researchers initially discovered, they were able to identify images of real children in the new ads.

These included sexual content depicting a minor belonging to a European royal family, transforming an officially released photograph into a video of a “graphic sex act.” The researchers are not naming the royal to protect the victim and say they contacted officials in the country. WIRED confirmed the source image came from the official website of a royal family.

“What we’re talking about here is not simply AI-generated child sex abuse material,” says Katie Paul, the director of the TTP. The researcher says it appears some images have been taken from the web before being used in the ads. “There’s a lot of harm that can come from this all while Meta is raking in money in the process.”

Overall, the researchers discovered that Meta has published more than 350 of the abusive video ads since the end of last year, with many of them linking to harmful harmful “nudification” apps linked to Chinese developers. In each instance, the researchers immediately reported the ads to US child safety authorities and through Meta’s reporting tools when ads were live and being shown to users at the time of their discovery. The researchers shared detailed findings with WIRED, which independently identified hundreds of other related “nudification” ads containing explicit content of adults on Meta’s platforms.

While the child abuse ads have now been removed for violating Meta’s policies on child exploitation, adult exploitation, and nudity, all of the ads were originally published despite the company’s policies saying it reviews all ads that run on its platforms. In some instances, the TTP researchers say, it took Meta a week to review live ads they had reported for containing CSAM with Meta’s tools. During that time, the ads racked up hundreds more views, according to screenshots seen by WIRED.

When some ads containing child sexual abuse were removed, TTP says, they did not initially include disclosures indicating that they violated Meta’s child sexual abuse policies; those details only appeared to be added after WIRED asked Meta about the discrepancy.

The cache of video ads published across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, and Meta’s broader advertising network since the end of last year follow similar patterns. Many include an innocuous picture of a preteen or teenage girl—only one contained a boy, according to the researchers—and overlaid text saying it is “not just a photo” and “there are no restriction” [sic] on what can be done with the image. When the seconds-long video ads start playing, the children’s faces are morphed into graphic sexual videos, often showing them performing sex acts. When clicked, the ads directed people to download AI-face swapping or video apps from Apple and Google’s app stores. “This is the AI that men actually use,” many of the ads say.

Paul says the researchers were able to find the real-world identities of four minors whose images were used in the ads, three of which are from the US. “There were several photos from the same teen who has a social media influencer account on one of Meta’s platforms,” Paul says. The second instance involved another teen influencer who had a public account, the researcher says. “One was a stock photo model that was a real person,” Paul says of the third instance. “It was actually labeled as pre-teen on the stock photo websites.” The final instance was the European royal family member.

The researchers reported all of the ads they found to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which allows people to report online child sexual abuse material, and say they are consulting on how to appropriately disclose their discoveries to the those impacted.

The ads were collectively shown to more than 29,000 accounts in countries across the European Union, plus around 7,000 accounts in the United Kingdom, according to data in Meta’s ad library, which shows live and archived ads, including the harmful ads that were no longer being shown to people. The ads were likely seen by thousands more people than Meta’s ad library indicates, with more than 250 of them appearing in the United States, 120 in Australia, and 80 in India, where Meta does not publish granular ad performance data.

“We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” says Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton. The company has previously removed hundreds of thousands of ads for violating its policies on nudification. The statement claims that “many” of the ads found by the researchers had already been removed and most had fewer than 200 impressions, with the company receiving “under $5,000” in ad payments.

In an email to WIRED, Meta says it reports child exploitation content to NCMEC and is reporting the ads to the organization. Meta minimized the findings by saying that the AI-generated videos featured adults and the clips of the minors were brief or blurred, which made detection of the content more difficult. “The criminals behind this activity know we’ve built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something,” Clayton says.

The TTP researchers’ discovery of hundreds of ads containing child abuse material comes amid Meta paying up to $16.7 billion to settle lawsuits over its social networks allegedly harming children. Meta is also appealing a New Mexico court decision that, if enacted, would require it to improve its CSAM reporting processes and include human reviews in the state.

Multiple lawmakers and regulators now say they are investigating or looking into the ads following WIRED’s reporting. “It is disappointing that Meta continues to run ads featuring child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual intimate images after it was brought to their attention,” says Virginia senator Mark Warner, who sent Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg a letter following WIRED’s initial reporting. The letter has not been replied to yet, according to Warner’s office. “Meta needs to follow their own advertising standards, heed the call, and put an end to these illegal and inappropriate ads,” he says. (Meta tells WIRED it will reply to the letter).

A spokesperson for Michigan’s attorney general says their office “is aware of reports concerning AI‑generated child sexual abuse material appearing in advertising on Meta. This is extremely troubling, and we are actively looking into the matter.” Similarly, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier posted on X that his office is “investigating.”

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Australia’s eSafety internet regulator says it is “highly concerned” by the reports and that it is assessing Meta’s compliance with its rules. It says it has requested “information on this matter from the company at a senior level.”

Lacking Protections

Over the last six years, dozens of AI nudification or “undress” apps and websites have flourished online, with them being used to harm countless women and girls. As this dangerous nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) ecosystem has continued to grow, with those behind it estimated to be earning millions each year, child protection organizations have warned the technology is “increasingly” used to create CSAM.

“AI apps are making it far too easy to create realistic criminal imagery of child sexual abuse, creating the new risk of everyday photos of children being taken and transformed into sexual content,” says Emma Hardy, director of communications at the Internet Watch Foundation, a UK-based nonprofit which removes child abuse content from the web. “Platforms and companies must make sure there is nowhere these apps can be advertised and spread.”

As WIRED previously reported, some of the ads discovered by TTP researchers were posted by Chinese companies that act as ad “resellers” in the country, where Meta’s platforms are banned. Many of the apps the ads linked to also appear to have Chinese connections, according to TTP. (Meta has previously launched legal action against a Hong Kong-based company linked to one set of nudifier platforms).

The ads pointed people towards almost 50 apps combined across Google’s Play Store and Apple’s App Store. Of the 350 ads, the researchers say that around 300 of them directed people to AI image or video generator ads, with most of these apps being linked to China-based developers. Some apps had already been removed by the time WIRED started reporting this story.

Among those that would generate explicit imagery of adults were eight identical apps listed on Apple’s App Store, multiple of which were linked to Chinese developer names. When the apps opened, they would show explicit AI-generated content, including a menu of sexual scenarios, including one called “threatening knife” where a knife is held to a woman’s throat. WIRED identified another seven identical apps that shared the same design, explicit content, and listed the same developer contact details.

“The App Store was designed to be a safe and trusted place for users, and we have zero tolerance for developers who deliberately attempt to evade our review process,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema. “The developers mentioned in this report initially submitted apps that are compliant with the App Review Guidelines, only to later surface nudify capabilities, which are against our rules.” The company says that 17 of the 20 apps included in the research had already been removed from its store and it has taken action against the remaining three, as well as removing the seven apps WIRED found.

Google spokesperson Dan Jackson says the company does not allow apps that contain sexual content or the ability to nudify. “We continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content,” they say, adding that it removed all the apps included in the report. “When violations are reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in the case of these apps has included suspending hundreds of violating apps and restricting related search terms like ‘nudify’ on our store.”

“The share of Chinese developers creating nudify apps has grown year over year,” says David Pham, a former Meta employee who investigated nonconsensual imagery and abuse on its platforms. Pham says that while at Meta he observed similar ads to those discovered by the researchers and those uploading the content would constantly try to get around safety systems.

“Every time the platform or investigators would build a new detection model or a new way to have some type of enforcement, they quickly—within a day, maybe five days—built a new way to avoid detection,” Pham says. Those uploading the ads would change domains they used, obscure who posted them, and include measures such as blurring imagery or subtly changing images to avoid detection. However, Pham, who left Meta last year, says it has the funding and resources to be able to tackle the uploads. “I would like to live in a world where we’re not getting CSAM or NCII material sent directly to our phones,” he says.

Meta’s current protections against ads containing CSAM and NCII appear to need work. More than 11,000 undress ads have appeared on Meta’s platforms since February this year, according to a recent Indicator Media report, with many of these being reportedly posted by “repeat offenders.” Analysis by WIRED also found hundreds of ads including explicit content that contain similar language to those ads found by the TTP researchers. (Meta says malicious advertisers use adversarial tactics to continually try to avoid its detection systems and it has “incorporated” the language in the ads highlighted by WIRED into its moderation systems.)

One ad containing one of the teenagers that the researchers found the real-world identity of was reported to Meta when it had reached four accounts in Europe, according to the TTPs research. However, when it was removed days later, it had been seen by more than 330 users. “This is not something that it should take a small nonprofit doing research to stumble across and then have to investigate and report,” Paul from TTP says. “We’re talking about one of the most well-resourced— technologically and financially—companies on the planet.”

entries.title: How NASA Testing Changed US Food Inspection Forever
entries.summary: In the early 20th century, public outcry following Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle led to stricter food safety protocols. NASA took them a step further.
entries.content:
In 1906, in response to public outcry that came after Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle detailed the revolting conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking plants, the US government passed the Federal Meat Inspection Act. The legislation created what would become known as the Food Safety and Inspection Service, a force of federal employees who would spend their days in stockyards and packing plants, checking livestock for disease both before and after their slaughter. They did their work organoleptically—with their eyes, noses, and hands—an approach soon dubbed “poke and sniff.” This 100 percent testing method worked well enough for spotting the lesions that signaled tuberculosis and cysticercosis (a tissue infection caused by tapeworms), and the federal presence discouraged plants from using illegal preservatives and generally unsanitary practices.

But by the end of the 20th century, as American taste for beef mushroomed, the system was clearly and woefully inadequate. The gotta-catch-’em-all approach was no match for plants butchering hundreds of animals an hour. The bigger problem was that testing had once more fallen behind in the arms race. Decades of poking at hearts, bile ducts, spleens, lungs, lymph nodes, livers, and kidneys had effectively rid the country’s meat supply of diseases that could be spotted or sniffed out. But humans can’t see, smell, or feel Escherichia coli.

In 1993, the growing danger of E. coli made itself evident when hamburgers sold by Jack in the Box fast-food restaurants sickened more than 700 people and killed four children. The public outcry rivaled the one sparked by The Jungle and triggered two moves by the Food Safety and Inspection Service. As a short-term fix, it hired 160 extra meat inspectors. More importantly, it accelerated a change in approach that had been bubbling away in the background ever since NASA decided it was time to send astronauts to space for more than a few hours at a time—long enough for them to get hungry.

That happened in the early 1960s, when the Mercury program, which first put Americans into space, gave way to Gemini, which proved out the equipment and procedures necessary for the longer, moon-bound Apollo missions to follow. Sending astronauts into space for multiple days meant dealing with the various elements of sustenance in zero gravity, from swallowing to defecating. But it was the middle step, digesting, that most worried Paul Lachance, the space agency’s lead food scientist. Food poisoning on Earth is terrible. In a spacesuit or space capsule, it could be catastrophic.

The obvious approach would be a 100 percent testing route, screening every morsel for pathogens and taking a zero-tolerance attitude. This was unworkable, because, as with artillery shells, every bite of food that’s tested is one that can’t be eaten. This is known as “destructive testing.” Proving a given batch was absolutely safe would involve eliminating most of it. Private industry was no help; what inspection did take place in the 1960s was far from scientific or suitable for NASA’s needs. Most pathogens were “discovered” by the people who consumed them.

Lachance and his colleagues responded by creating a new way of testing food safety. Where Walter Shewhart’s control chart was a tool for spotting manufacturing issues that could then be resolved, they conceived of an approach that went further, proactively identifying all the points where problems are most likely to start, and focusing inspection there. The core idea was to test food not after it was produced, but to so control its production that such testing was unnecessary. They called it Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point, today better known as HACCP.

To help digest this, think of basic acceptance sampling as the bit of wine the waiter has you taste so you know the bottle hasn’t spoiled before everyone gets a full glass. The basic Shewhart approach, then, is like the “test pancake” you make as you’re starting up breakfast. It tells you whether your production process, which requires a batter of the right consistency and a griddle at the right temperature, is on track. HACCP (pronounced hassip) is more like the way you should make a soup. Each time you add salt or broth or lemon juice or cream, you taste it to see how the flavor, saltiness, and acidity match what you’re aiming for.

For NASA, analyzed hazards could be physical (crystallized Tang powder could break a tooth), chemical (the presence of pesticide residues), or microbiological (the pathogens that posed the most serious threat in space). A critical control point could be any moment or action in the production process, from gathering raw materials to vacuum-sealing a package. “We identified the critical steps that would make the difference between something being safe or not safe,” Lachance said. “The temperature, the pressure, whatever that criteria was, whatever that critical control point was.” A chicken headed into space would be plucked, deboned, cut into pieces small enough to freeze-dry, and cooked, at which point it would be sterile. But as various people handled it, the meat would be checked on its way to the freeze dryer, then on its way into plastic packaging, then again after being vacuum-sealed. To this day, no astronaut has gotten food poisoning while in space.

“HACCP introduced careful design, rigorous standards, and precise measurement into the largely intuitive, loosely organized, hit-or-miss world of industrial food safety prior to the 1970s,” Timothy D. Lytton wrote in his 2019 book about foodborne illness, Outbreak. Pillsbury, which produced crumble-free food for NASA (floating crumbs were also a concern in space) and had a major hand in developing HACCP, implemented the process into its own consumer production lines after 1971, when a Connecticut woman found glass in some of its baby cereal. The approach went national in 1973, when the FDA added HACCP-based rules to its regulation of low-acid canned foods, where botulism was an issue. The European arm of the World Health Organization recommended using HACCP in 1983, and in 1985 the National Academy of Sciences declared it better than “random testing of foods” (aka inspection).

In 1996, three years after Jack in the Box’s E. coli–speckled hamburgers made all those people sick, the Food Safety and Inspection Service demanded that America’s meat processing plants get with the program. By 2004, illness from E. coli had dropped 42 percent, reaching a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention goal six years ahead of schedule. In 2011, the Food Safety Modernization Act required that all US food manufacturers develop and stick to HACCP-based safety plans.

Among experts, this way of thinking about food safety is as established as quality control is in manufacturing. “The testing of finished products for food safety is foolishness,” says Larry Keener, president and CEO of International Product Safety Consultants. He’s looking forward to the potential of new technology, including machine learning and genome sequencing, to make HACCP even more effective. But like all testing, HACCP’s usefulness depends on how it’s used. “Unfortunately, the industry and the regulatory community have, in my estimation, been slow to catch on and pick up and use this powerful strategy to improve the safety of the food supply,” Keener says.

Indeed, every year, foodborne disease sickens 48 million people—that’s one in six Americans—puts 128,000 in the hospital, and kills 3,000. Those numbers are stubborn for a couple of reasons. Food safety is hard to see, so it’s hard for manufacturers to make it a differentiator. And while consumers may say they value safety above all, in reality price and convenience tend to win out, especially when it’s not clear what’s safe and what isn’t. The combined result is that manufacturers have little incentive to make more than the minimum effort. Meanwhile, the FDA (which oversees most food that isn’t meat) isn’t much of a task master. When it does run inspections, it’s focused on verifying that manufacturers can provide the proper documentation of their safety plan.

“They’ll show up maybe once every couple of years. Or if a particular sector starts to cause a lot of foodborne illness, FDA will focus on that more. But usually it’s reactive,” says Denis Stearns, a founding partner at food-safety-focused law firm Marler Clark. “It’s only if you cause a big outbreak, then they also come in and do their own testing … They’re like the fire department. You don’t see them until your house is on fire.”

Yet we have evidence that stricter standards and tighter testing can work. Since the 1960s, the French government has allowed certain manufacturers to slap the “Label Rouge” on their products, signifying that they have gone far beyond the legal minimum for quality and safety. It’s applied to all sorts of products, but is most closely associated with chicken. Its HACCP-like quality control process includes 65 individual tests, strict requirements on how much space and what kind of food the animals get, and—this being France—regular taste tests by experts and consumers to ensure the result is “vividly distinguishable” from the non-label version. Label Rouge chickens tend to cost twice as much as the regular birds, but make up one-third of sales and have a drastically lower salmonella rate than those in conventional flocks.

entries.title: 5 Best Smart Speakers (2026): Alexa, Google, Apple
entries.summary: Looking to add a smart speaker to your house? Here’s which to choose, whether you’re an Alexa, Siri, or Gemini fan.
entries.content:
There are three big players in the running for the best smart speaker: Amazon, Google, and Apple. Each voice-assistant-powered system has its own benefits and limitations, and you’ll have to consider several factors to pinpoint the right smart speaker for your needs.

You may already have a favorite ecosystem. Maybe it's the one that’s compatible with your phone, as an Apple or Android user. Or maybe it's Amazon's Alexa, if you already own one of the many speakers that the company launched following the 2014 arrival of the first Amazon Echo. Amazon's smart-speaker fleet, in particular, is expansive, often seeing multiple new models every year, while the offerings are much narrower for Google and Apple. That said, a few months ago, Google did launch a new smart speaker for the first time in years—the 2026 Google Home Speaker—and I share my thoughts on it in this guide.

After trying nearly every single smart speaker that's come out in the last decade, I have a sense of the best options available today to fit various needs. Also, check out my guides to the Best Alexa Speakers, Best Google Speakers, and Best Smart Displays if you want more insight into each category.

Updated September 2026: I've added details about Amazon’s increased prices and which speakers were affected, and noted that the Google Nest Hub Max is currently out of stock online.

The Best Smart Speakers

Best for Google Users

Google's latest smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker (8/10, WIRED Recommends), is an amalgamation of great features from other smart speakers. It shares its name with the original Google speaker from 2016, but its shape and size are reminiscent of an Apple HomePod Mini. It has the tap controls and fun colors I remember from the older Google Nest Mini. And it joins the rest of Google’s smart speakers (other than the Google Pixel Tablet with the charging dock) by using Google Gemini as the default assistant instead of Google Assistant.

Gemini does sound impressively human, offering answers that approximate an interaction with another person. Sometimes its answers get a little long-winded, so just be prepared for that. But Google Gemini is nonetheless a touch smarter than other assistants in its cohort; it’s able to answer questions about my own schedule and knows to check with me about my artist preference if a song I request has multiple covers.

Gemini for Home is free, but some features you might like to use are hidden behind paywalls. For instance, Google rebranded its video camera subscriptions to “Google Home Premium,” which bundles some smart-home assistant features and video storage into one price. There are two tiers: Standard ($10 per month or $100 per year), which includes 30 days of event-based video history, intelligent alerts for things like familiar faces and packages, Gemini Live, and an AI-based tool to help you create smart-home routines for your household. The Advanced tier ($20 per month or $200 per year) includes 60 days of event-based video history, 10 days of 24/7 video history, descriptive notifications, searchable video history, video event descriptions, and daily summaries of recorded events, plus everything in the cheaper plan.

Gemini Live is the main behind-the-paywall feature you might want; it lets you switch your smart speaker into a more conversational mode. Using this feature, I had a long, natural-feeling chat with my speaker that covered my 3-year-old’s sleep patterns, scalp sunburns, and the previous night’s Love Island episode. It worked well, but it's not a capability I imagine I’ll use when I'm not actively testing.

Gemini Live doesn't work on every Google speaker, but in addition to working on the Google Home Speaker, it also works on all three versions of its available smart displays, including two iterations of the Nest Hub. My favorite is the 10-inch Nest Hub Max; it doubles as a digital photo frame powered by Google Photos, which works much better than Amazon's clunky uploader and might even be a tool you're already using. Google accounts get up to 15 GB of free storage (that'll include any Gmail or Drive files, too), so there are a lot of photos you can store and display on this device.

The Nest Hub Max has a solid sound profile given its slim frame with two 10-watt tweeters and a 30-watt woofer. The 10-inch touchscreen is a great size for everything from controlling your smart home and streaming videos to pulling up recipes and enjoying your own photos. Many of these capabilities rely on the smart display, which means you couldn't access them with a screen-free smart speaker. It's not the only smart display option on the market, but it has a prettier interface than Amazon's Echo Show 11 (below), and unlike on the Show 11, you won't see any ads sliding onto the screen on this Nest. There's also a camera for video calls and gesture-based controls. While there’s no cover for the camera, you can disable it if you prefer.

However, the Nest Hub Max seems to be completely out of stock at all retailers. I'm hoping we see it return, or get news of a new version. But we'll have to wait and see.

Best for Amazon Users

Most of the smart speakers I spot in friends' homes come from the Amazon Echo line. Options abound, and many that I see are older models, like the puck-shaped Echo Dot. Such dated speakers are still fairly well-supported, though not all of them can gain access to Alexa+, Amazon's newer AI-powered voice assistant. But even if your smart speaker can use Alexa+, it's only worth the upgrade if you have Amazon Prime, which includes access to the assistant. Without a Prime subscription, you'd have to pay $20 a month for Alexa+ on its own. It's literally cheaper to get Amazon Prime ($15 a month for most plans), which comes with a wider range of benefits. This price model is surely intentional, as it may serve as a push to get you to sign up for Prime if you haven't already.

The Echo Dot Max is one of Amazon's newest models. It launched in late 2025, taking the small form from past Dot models and upgrading the device with impressive sound quality, a built-in smart-home hub, Alexa and Alexa+ access, and a slightly different look. It’s surprisingly loud without getting muddled, especially considering its small size. Impressively, it can still hear my requests even when the room is loud or it is playing loud music. I tested it against the latest Echo Studio last year and found the speakers were more similar in quality than I expected. The Dot Max is more expensive than older Dot models; if you don’t need next-level sound, the more affordable Echo Dot (fifth gen) might be a good fit for your needs.

Both the Echo Dot Max and the Echo Dot were hit by price increases at the end of August. Amazon raised prices across its product categories, including its Echo speakers. The Echo Dot Max got a $20 increase and a new $120 price tag, while the Echo Dot (5th Gen) went from $50 to $80. I'm most disappointed about the Echo Dot, since now its sale prices will likely only go down to the $50 range instead of landing between $25 and $30. It makes it a less appealing buy at its new price, and I recommend waiting for a sale for both of these models.

If you're looking for something with more capabilities, like being able to read recipes, stream shows, and even make video calls, you might want a smart display instead of a smart speaker. These devices can perform the same functions as any other smart speaker, but they add a screen and camera to unlock a variety of new abilities.

Amazon launched two new smart displays last fall: The Echo Show 11 ($250) is the pricier of the two, but I liked it better than the new Echo Show 8 ($200). The Show 11 has better sound, and its 11-inch screen was a nice size for both my desk and kitchen counter. The interface is updated for Alexa+, but I didn’t love some of the changes. For instance, when you ask Alexa+ questions, the Show 11 brings up a chat-like interface. Because of this, some answers don’t provide the same level of detail as I got with the original Alexa. The change that I like the least is how Alexa+ handles the weather; I loved seeing the pages of weather info for the day and week that original Alexa would show, and now I just get a small snippet in a sea of written words. If you want something similar but cheaper, I'd recommend the older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) over the newest one. That model had a better sound when I tested both Echo Show 8 versions side by side.

It's also important to note that Echo Show devices have a lot of screen clutter, and the devices also show ads. You might not see the ads right away, but eventually you'll start seeing prompts to buy things on Amazon. You can activate photo mode to hide the ads, but that will only last three hours before going back to regular mode. You can also remove clutter (like the multiple news, sports, and food-related topics it'll show by default) by going into the device's settings. An Echo Show device can technically double as a digital photo frame, but it's annoying to upload pictures and won't put vertical photos side-by-side.

Neither the Echo Show 11 nor the older Echo Show 8 increased in price like the Echo Dot Max, but the newer Echo Show 8 did and is now retailing for a base price of $200. It's on sale right now to match the price of the older model, though, so that's a pro for now. The new prices really just make my two preferred options an even better buy than before—just a $20 increase to get the Echo Show 11 over the new Show 8 is well worth the better sound and larger screen.

Best for Apple Users

Smart speaker options are the most limited for Apple users. My colleagues and I weren’t impressed by the sound quality of the larger HomePod when it relaunched in 2023. But the smaller HomePod Mini is a fine investment for the price, and you'll find it to be the most convenient option if you already use the Apple Home app and Siri.

It's about a third of the price and smaller than the full-size speaker; otherwise, it’s capable of just about everything the larger model can do. It doubles as a smart home hub to connect your Apple-compatible devices, so you don't need the larger speaker or Apple TV if you're mainly looking for smart-home control. It's still not my favorite smart speaker overall, and Apple HomeKit isn't my favorite ecosystem. It has serious limitations, and I find myself running into more issues adding my devices to the Home app than on any other platform. But if you're committed to your Apple ecosystem, this is the speaker to buy.

There's also no smart display option in Apple's ecosystem, so if you'd like one of those in your home, you'll have to go with Google or Apple. Notably, Apple's price hikes in June affected both the Apple HomePod Mini and the larger HomePod. The HomePod Mini used to be $99 but now retails for $129.
